extracted.intended_audience: civic technologists, policy makers, agency rulemaking staff, and public commenters interested in using social media to engage in rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how agencies and commenters can incorporate social media into administrative rulemaking to broaden and structure public participation, while preserving substantive input channels (e.g., Regulations.gov filings paired with public threads).

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace New Participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must 'adapt to what rulemaking newcomers can provide' without dismissing traditional expert evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Cornell Law School study emphasized that agencies should recognize and incorporate contributions from newcomers to rulemaking (e.g., everyday experience, community perspectives) while still valuing and weighing established technical/expert submissions. Design outreach and intake to accept and surface non‑traditional forms of input rather than excluding them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Crowdsourcing Principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Use crowdsourcing mechanisms (model: Reddit's voting) to surface meaningful comments while filtering noise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt features that surface high‑value contributions and deprioritize low‑value noise so officials see diverse public perspectives. Example mechanism cited: Reddit voting to highlight salient comments. The goal is to expose officials to representative and substantive viewpoints without requiring them to wade through all raw volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance Accessibility with Substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide accessible input channels that still produce meaningful, substantive input without overwhelming officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the tension between opening participation (lower barriers, social media formats) and ensuring comment quality; design processes and interfaces that make it easy for newcomers to contribute useful information and that prevent officials from being overwhelmed. The blog argues benefits outweigh implementation difficulties, but agencies must plan to manage volume and maintain substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Social Media to Refine Existing Platforms (e.g., Regulations.gov)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage social media to enhance—not replace—formal comment platforms by creating structured dialogue that highlights experiential knowledge and controversial issues alongside technical expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate social threads with formal portals so social discussions feed into the official record or help prioritize what officials read. Emphasize structuring conversations to surface experiential accounts and contentious topics while still linking back to technical submissions on official platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Couple Regulations.gov Filings with Public Social Media Threads
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters should pair an official Regulations.gov filing with a public social media thread to amplify and structure dialogue around their submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactical recommendation for commenters: file the formal comment and run a parallel social media thread that summarizes, highlights key points, and drives discussion—creating a 'highlight reel' version that can attract attention and clarify the substance of the formal filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess Legal and Policy Barriers Before Integrating Social Media
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore and address legal and policy constraints to incorporating social media into rulemaking processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACUS's Committee on Rulemaking examined these barriers; agencies should investigate statutory, procedural, and recordkeeping issues before adopting social media tools, and develop policies that enable 'appropriate and innovative' uses consistent with administrative law requirements.
